claim: The segmentation gene network in insects can produce equivalent phenotypic outputs despite differences in upstream regulatory inputs between species.
source: The segmentation gene network in insects can produce equivalent phenotypic outputs despite differences in upstream regulatory inputs between species.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about the segmentation gene network.

claim: Initiation and dynamics of gap gene expression differ markedly between M. abdita and Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Initiation and dynamics of gap gene expression differ markedly between M. abdita and Drosophila melanogaster, while the output of the system converges to equivalent patterns at the end of the blastoderm stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative expression data presented in the manuscript comparing the two species.

claim: The output of the gap gene system converges to equivalent patterns at the end of the blastoderm stage in M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Initiation and dynamics of gap gene expression differ markedly between M. abdita and Drosophila melanogaster, while the output of the system converges to equivalent patterns at the end of the blastoderm stage.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data showing convergence of gap domain positions by late blastoderm stage.

claim: The qualitative structure of the gap gene network is conserved between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Although the qualitative structure of the gap gene network is conserved, there are differences in the strength of regulatory interactions between species.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi knock-down experiments showing similar types of regulatory interactions in both species.

claim: There are differences in the strength of regulatory interactions in the gap gene network between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Although the qualitative structure of the gap gene network is conserved, there are differences in the strength of regulatory interactions between species.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of RNAi knock-down effects showing altered interaction strengths.

claim: Quantitative system drift provides a mechanistic explanation for the developmental hourglass model in the dipteran lineage.
source: It provides a mechanistic explanation for the developmental hourglass model in the dipteran lineage.
evidence: This is based on the observation that early expression differs but converges later, consistent with the hourglass model.

claim: Quantitative system drift is likely to be a widespread mechanism for developmental evolution.
source: Quantitative system drift is likely to be a widespread mechanism for developmental evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings in the gap gene system.

claim: The gap gene system constitutes the first regulatory layer of the segmentation gene network.
source: In this study, we use the dipteran gap gene system—constituting the first regulatory layer of the segmentation gene network (Foe and Alberts, 1983; Akam, 1987; Ingham, 1988; Jaeger, 2011)—as a model system to study developmental system drift.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on the segmentation gene network.

claim: Gap genes receive regulatory inputs from maternal protein gradients formed by bicoid (bcd), hunchback (hb), and caudal (cad).
source: Gap genes receive regulatory inputs from maternal protein gradients formed by the gene products of bicoid (bcd), hunchback (hb), and caudal (cad) (Figure 1, top row of graphs) (reviewed in St Johnston and Nüsslein-Volhard (1992)).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review and by Figure 1 showing the maternal gradients.

claim: Maternal gradients set up an initial asymmetry along the antero-posterior axis of the embryo.
source: These gradients set up an initial asymmetry along the major or antero-posterior (A–P) axis of the embryo.
evidence: This is established knowledge about maternal gradients in Drosophila development.

claim: Bcd and Cad activate the four trunk gap genes hb, Krüppel (Kr), knirps (kni), and giant (gt).
source: Bcd and Cad activate the four trunk gap genes hb, Krüppel (Kr), knirps (kni), and giant (gt), which become expressed in broad, overlapping domains (Figure 1, bottom row of graphs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap gene regulation, supported by Figure 1.

claim: Gap gene cross-repression refines the pattern as development proceeds.
source: As development proceeds, gap gene cross-repression refines the pattern (Figure 1, grey inset) (see Jaeger, 2011 for review).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Domains of hb and kni have mutually exclusive expression patterns and show strong mutual repression.
source: Domains of hb and kni as well as Kr and gt have mutually exclusive expression patterns and show strong mutual repression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap gene interactions in D. melanogaster.

claim: Domains of Kr and gt have mutually exclusive expression patterns and show strong mutual repression.
source: Domains of hb and kni as well as Kr and gt have mutually exclusive expression patterns and show strong mutual repression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap gene interactions in D. melanogaster.

claim: The 'alternating cushions' mechanism maintains and sharpens the basic staggered arrangement of gap domains.
source: This 'alternating cushions' mechanism maintains and sharpens the basic staggered arrangement of gap domains.
evidence: This is a conceptual description of the regulatory mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: The expression patterns of Kr/kni, kni/gt, and gt/hb overlap and show weaker repression with a posterior-to-anterior bias.
source: The expression patterns of Kr/kni, kni/gt, and gt/hb overlap and show weaker repression with a posterior-to-anterior bias, which results in anterior shifts of each of these domains over time.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap gene interactions in D. melanogaster.

claim: Weaker repression with posterior-to-anterior bias results in anterior shifts of gap domains over time.
source: The expression patterns of Kr/kni, kni/gt, and gt/hb overlap and show weaker repression with a posterior-to-anterior bias, which results in anterior shifts of each of these domains over time.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap gene dynamics in D. melanogaster.

claim: Trunk gap gene expression is repressed in the posterior pole region by the terminal gap genes tailless (tll) and huckebein (hkb).
source: Finally, trunk gap gene expression is repressed in the posterior pole region of the embryo by the terminal gap genes tailless (tll) and huckebein (hkb).
evidence: This is established knowledge about terminal gap gene function in D. melanogaster.

claim: M. abdita belongs to the brachyceran infra-order Cyclorrhapha.
source: M. abdita belongs to the brachyceran infra-order Cyclorrhapha (marked in red)
evidence: This is a taxonomic classification shown in Figure 1.

claim: Only cyclorrhaphan flies have a bcd gene.
source: Only cyclorrhaphan flies have a bcd gene.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend and is established knowledge about bicoid evolution.

claim: Posterior patterning is delayed in the moth midge Clogmia albipunctata.
source: Qualitative (Rohr et al., 1999; García-Solache et al., 2010; Jiménez-Guri et al., 2014) and quantitative (Crombach et al., 2014; Janssens et al., 2014) studies of segmentation gene expression in the moth midge Clogmia albipunctata (family: Psychodidae) indicate that posterior patterning—especially the onset of posterior hb expression—is delayed
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on C. albipunctata.

claim: Repression between Kr and gt may not be conserved in Clogmia albipunctata, which lacks a posterior gt domain.
source: and that repression between Kr and gt may not be conserved in this species, which lacks a posterior gt domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of the posterior gt domain in C. albipunctata.

claim: A posterior delay in gap gene expression is observed in the malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae.
source: A similar posterior delay is observed in the malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae (Culicidae), where both posterior domains of hb and gt are present, but appear only after gastrulation in an A–P order which is reversed compared to that observed in D. melanogaster (Goltsev et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on A. gambiae.

claim: In Anopheles gambiae, posterior domains of hb and gt appear only after gastrulation in an A–P order which is reversed compared to D. melanogaster.
source: A similar posterior delay is observed in the malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae (Culicidae), where both posterior domains of hb and gt are present, but appear only after gastrulation in an A–P order which is reversed compared to that observed in D. melanogaster (Goltsev et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on A. gambiae.

claim: There is no maternal contribution to hb expression in the marmalade hoverfly Episyrphus balteatus.
source: One of these is the marmalade hoverfly Episyrphus balteatus (Syrphidae). In this species, the pattern and order of gap gene activation along the A–P axis is largely conserved compared to D. melanogaster, even though there is no maternal contribution to hb expression (Figure 1) (Lemke and Schmidt-Ott, 2009; Lemke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on E. balteatus and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The pattern and order of gap gene activation along the A–P axis is largely conserved in Episyrphus balteatus compared to D. melanogaster.
source: In this species, the pattern and order of gap gene activation along the A–P axis is largely conserved compared to D. melanogaster, even though there is no maternal contribution to hb expression (Figure 1) (Lemke and Schmidt-Ott, 2009; Lemke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on E. balteatus.

claim: Maternal transcripts of bcd and hb can be detected in M. abdita.
source: Maternal transcripts of bcd and hb can be detected (Stauber et al., 1999, 2000; Lemke et al., 2008), but no maternal contribution to cad expression is present in this species (Stauber et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on M. abdita.

claim: No maternal contribution to cad expression is present in M. abdita.
source: Maternal transcripts of bcd and hb can be detected (Stauber et al., 1999, 2000; Lemke et al., 2008), but no maternal contribution to cad expression is present in this species (Stauber et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on M. abdita.

claim: Localised maternal bcd transcripts at the anterior pole extend further posterior in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: Localised maternal bcd transcripts at the anterior pole extend further posterior, and bcd RNAi cuticle phenotypes affect more posterior segments than in D. melanogaster, indicating a broader role of Bcd in M. abdita (Stauber et al., 1999, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on M. abdita.

claim: bcd RNAi cuticle phenotypes affect more posterior segments in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: Localised maternal bcd transcripts at the anterior pole extend further posterior, and bcd RNAi cuticle phenotypes affect more posterior segments than in D. melanogaster, indicating a broader role of Bcd in M. abdita (Stauber et al., 1999, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on M. abdita.

claim: Bcd has a broader role in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: Localised maternal bcd transcripts at the anterior pole extend further posterior, and bcd RNAi cuticle phenotypes affect more posterior segments than in D. melanogaster, indicating a broader role of Bcd in M. abdita (Stauber et al., 1999, 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on the broader distribution and phenotypic effects of bcd in M. abdita.

claim: Expression of maternal and zygotic hb appears very similar in M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: In contrast, expression of maternal and zygotic hb appears very similar in both species (Stauber et al., 2000; Lemke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The zygotic anterior hb domain is severely depleted in M. abdita embryos treated with bcd RNAi.
source: The zygotic anterior hb domain is severely depleted in embryos treated with bcd RNAi, suggesting activation of hb by Bcd as in D. melanogaster (Lemke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on M. abdita.

claim: Bcd activates hb in M. abdita as in D. melanogaster.
source: The zygotic anterior hb domain is severely depleted in embryos treated with bcd RNAi, suggesting activation of hb by Bcd as in D. melanogaster (Lemke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAi phenotype and comparison to D. melanogaster.

claim: Cuticle phenotypes of hb RNAi-treated M. abdita embryos resemble hb hypomorphs in D. melanogaster.
source: Moreover, the regulatory role of hb seems to be similar as well, since cuticle phenotypes of hb RNAi-treated M. abdita embryos resemble hb hypomorphs in D. melanogaster (Stauber et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on M. abdita.

claim: The regulatory role of hb is similar in M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Moreover, the regulatory role of hb seems to be similar as well, since cuticle phenotypes of hb RNAi-treated M. abdita embryos resemble hb hypomorphs in D. melanogaster (Stauber et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of cuticle phenotypes.

claim: The early embryonic transcriptome of M. abdita has been sequenced.
source: As a foundation for such an analysis we have previously sequenced the early embryonic transcriptome of M. abdita (Jiménez-Guri et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: A precise staging scheme for M. abdita embryogenesis has been established with a focus on the blastoderm stage.
source: and have established a precise staging scheme for embryogenesis—with a particular focus on the blastoderm stage (Wotton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Gap gene expression differs significantly between M. abdita and D. melanogaster during early to mid blastoderm stage.
source: Our comparison reveals that gap gene expression differs significantly between the two species during early to mid blastoderm stage but converges to equivalent patterns before the onset of gastrulation.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gap gene expression converges to equivalent patterns before the onset of gastrulation in M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Our comparison reveals that gap gene expression differs significantly between the two species during early to mid blastoderm stage but converges to equivalent patterns before the onset of gastrulation.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The broader influence of Bcd in M. abdita causes gap domains to emerge at more posterior positions compared to D. melanogaster.
source: In particular, we find that the broader influence of Bcd in M. abdita causes gap domains to emerge at more posterior positions compared to D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is an inference based on the broader bcd distribution and the observed posterior displacement of gap domains.

claim: The absence of maternal Cad causes a delay in the onset of anterior shifts of posterior gap domains in M. abdita.
source: In addition, the absence of maternal Cad causes a delay in the onset of anterior shifts of posterior gap domains in M. abdita.
evidence: This is supported by the cad germ-line clone experiments in D. melanogaster showing similar delays.

claim: The delay in anterior shifts of posterior gap domains is later compensated by stronger shifts compared to D. melanogaster.
source: This delay is later compensated by stronger shifts compared to D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data showing larger shifts in M. abdita.

claim: Qualitative regulatory structure is strongly conserved between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Our knock-down analysis reveals that qualitative regulatory structure—the type of interactions between gap genes—is strongly conserved between species.
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi knock-down experiments showing similar types of interactions.

claim: There are changes significantly affecting the strength of gap gene cross-repression between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: We do, however, detect changes significantly affecting the strength of gap gene cross-repression.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of RNAi knock-down effects.

claim: Quantitative developmental system drift is a common feature of evolving developmental systems.
source: Based on these considerations, quantitative system drift is likely to be important, not only for neutral phenotypic evolution but also for the de novo evolution of biological form.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings in the gap gene system.

claim: Embryos were classified by cleavage cycle (C10–14A) and eight separate time classes within C14A (T1–8).
source: Embryos were classified by cleavage cycle (C10–14A), and eight separate time classes within C14A (T1–8), according to the staging scheme in Wotton et al. (2014).
evidence: This describes the methodology used for temporal classification of embryos.

claim: The temporal resolution for expression data is around 20 min during C13 and 7 min for each time class during C14A.
source: This results in a temporal resolution for our expression data of around 20 min during C13 and 7 min for each time class during C14A.
evidence: This describes the temporal resolution achieved in the study.

claim: The M. abdita expression dataset consists of a total of 367 embryos.
source: Our M. abdita expression dataset consists of a total of 367 embryos (91 stained for hb, 83 for Kr, 87 for gt, and 106 for kni).
evidence: This is stated in the table legend describing the dataset.

claim: bcd transcripts extend from the anterior pole to 23% A–P position at C12 in M. abdita.
source: At C12, bcd transcripts extend from the anterior pole to 23% A–P position (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data and shown in Figure 10.

claim: bcd transcripts in M. abdita extend 9–12%EL further to the posterior than in D. melanogaster at C12.
source: This is 9–12%EL further to the posterior, or almost twice a far, as in D. melanogaster embryos at any time during the blastoderm stage (Berleth et al., 1988; Little et al., 2011; Crombach et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is based on comparison of quantitative data between species.

claim: bcd transcripts disappear at C14A-T2 in M. abdita, earlier than in D. melanogaster where they can still be detected up to C14A-T4.
source: bcd transcripts in M. abdita disappear at C14A-T2, earlier than in D. melanogaster where they can still be detected up to C14A-T4 (Figure 10) (Crombach et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is based on comparison of expression data between species.

claim: Zygotic cad transcripts are first detected at C12 in M. abdita extending from around 34% A–P position to the posterior pole.
source: We first detect zygotic cad transcripts at C12 extending from around 34% A–P position to the posterior pole (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data and shown in Figure 10.

claim: At C13, the anterior boundary of cad expression is at a similar position in M. abdita and D. melanogaster (31 vs 33% A–P position).
source: At C13, the anterior boundary of cad expression is at a similar position in M. abdita and D. melanogaster (31 vs 33% A–P position; Figure 10) (Crombach et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is based on comparison of quantitative data between species.

claim: cad retracts towards the posterior in D. melanogaster during C14A while it maintains a stationary boundary in M. abdita.
source: However, at subsequent stages, cad retracts towards the posterior in D. melanogaster (39–42% A–P position during C14A-T2 to T5), while it maintains a stationary boundary at around 31–32% A–P position in M. abdita (until around C14A-T5; Figure 10; see also Stauber et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on comparison of expression data between species.

claim: tll expression is first detected at C12 in M. abdita in a domain at the posterior pole extending to 90% A–P position.
source: We first detect tll expression at C12 in a domain at the posterior pole extending to 90% A–P position (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data and shown in Figure 10.

claim: The anterior tll domain appears in C13 in D. melanogaster but does not appear until around C14-T4 in M. abdita.
source: Expression dynamics in the anterior differ more markedly: while the anterior tll domain in D. melanogaster appears in C13, its equivalent in M. abdita does not appear until around C14-T4 (Figure 10) (Pignoni et al., 1990; Crombach et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is based on comparison of expression data between species.

claim: hkb expression is first detected at C12 in M. abdita in two domains, one at the anterior pole extending to 8% A–P position, and one at the posterior pole extending to 90% A–P position.
source: We first detect hkb expression at C12 in two domains, one at the anterior pole extending to 8% A–P position, and one at the posterior pole extending to 90% A–P position (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data and shown in Figure 10.

claim: An anterior domain of zygotic hb expression is first detected at C11 in M. abdita extending from 0 to 56% A–P position.
source: We first detect the formation of an anterior domain of zygotic hb expression in M. abdita at C11. This domain extends from 0 to 56% A–P position, reaching significantly further posterior than in D. melanogaster, where it is located from 0 to 50% A–P position (Figure 11) (Tautz, 1988; Crauk and Dostatni, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data and shown in Figure 11.

claim: The posterior boundary of the anterior hb domain steadily shifts to the anterior over time in M. abdita.
source: In M. abdita, the posterior boundary of the anterior hb domain steadily shifts to the anterior over time (Figure 11).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data and shown in Figure 11.

claim: The posterior boundary of the anterior hb domain remains stationary through C14A in D. melanogaster.
source: In contrast, the equivalent boundary in D. melanogaster remains stationary through C14A (see Figure 3) (Surkova et al., 2008a; Crombach et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is based on comparison to published data on D. melanogaster.

claim: gt expression is first detected at C12 in M. abdita in an anterior stripe at 14–34% A–P position and a posterior domain extending from 73% A–P position to the posterior pole.
source: We first detect gt expression in M. abdita at C12 in an anterior stripe at 14–34% A–P position, and a posterior domain extending from 73% A–P position to the posterior pole (Figure 11).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data and shown in Figure 11.

claim: Kr expression is first detected at C12 in M. abdita in a central domain between 40 and 63% A–P position.
source: In M. abdita, we first detect Kr expression at C12, as is the case in D. melanogaster (Knipple et al., 1985; Jaeger et al., 2007). Kr appears in a central domain between 40 and 63% A–P position (Figure 11).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data and shown in Figure 11.

claim: The central Kr domain is much wider at C12 in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster (23 vs 12%EL).
source: This domain is much wider at this stage than in D. melanogaster (23 vs 12%EL), extending further to the anterior (by 8.6% EL) and to the posterior (by 2.6% EL) (Knipple et al., 1985; Jaeger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on comparison of quantitative data between species.

claim: kni expression is first detected at C12 in M. abdita in the anterior pole region extending to 7% A–P position and in an abdominal domain at 61–78% A–P position.
source: We first detect kni expression at C12 in the anterior pole region extending to 7% A–P position and in an abdominal domain at 61–78% A–P position (Figure 11).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data and shown in Figure 11.

claim: Reduced levels of bcd in RNAi embryos result in an increasingly anterior position of the hb boundary in M. abdita.
source: We find that reduced levels of bcd in RNAi embryos result in an increasingly anterior position of the hb boundary in M. abdita (Figure 4), suggesting that the placement of gap domains is dependent on Bcd levels as in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is supported by the bcd RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The placement of gap domains is dependent on Bcd levels in M. abdita as in D. melanogaster.
source: We find that reduced levels of bcd in RNAi embryos result in an increasingly anterior position of the hb boundary in M. abdita (Figure 4), suggesting that the placement of gap domains is dependent on Bcd levels as in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is an inference based on the bcd RNAi results.

claim: D. melanogaster embryos lacking maternal cad but retaining one copy of zygotic cad exhibit posterior displacement of gt and kni domains as development proceeds during C14A.
source: The resulting embryos lack maternal, but retain one copy of zygotic, cad. They exhibit early initiation of posterior gt and kni expression within normal wild-type variability. However, as development proceeds during cleavage cycle 14A (C14A) these domains show substantial posterior displacement compared to the wild-type (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the cad germ-line clone experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Altered levels and timing of cad expression are responsible for the delayed shifts of posterior gap domains in M. abdita.
source: This suggests that altered levels and timing of cad expression are indeed responsible for the delayed shifts of posterior gap domains in M. abdita.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cad germ-line clone experiments.

claim: M. abdita hb knock-down results in deletion of the thorax, defects in abdominal segments A1–8 and A8, and a reduced cephalopharyngeal skeleton.
source: In M. abdita, hb knock-down (as previously published in Stauber et al., 2000) results in the deletion of the thorax, with additional defects in abdominal segments A1–8 and A8, and a reduced cephalopharyngeal skeleton, suggesting that the posterior gnathocephalon is also missing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study and describes the cuticle phenotype.

claim: M. abdita hb knock-down corresponds to a hypomorphic hb mutant phenotype in D. melanogaster.
source: This corresponds to a hypomorphic hb mutant phenotype in D. melanogaster (Nüsslein-Volhard and Wieschaus, 1980; Jürgens et al., 1984; Lehmann and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1987).
evidence: This is based on comparison to published D. melanogaster mutant phenotypes.

claim: M. abdita gt RNAi results in cuticles lacking abdominal segments A5–7.
source: M. abdita gt RNAi resulted in cuticles lacking abdominal segments A5–7 (Figure 12B) rather than just the denticle bands of abdominal segments A5–7 as in D. melanogaster (i.e., no naked cuticle is formed) (Wieschaus et al., 1984a; Gergen and Wieschaus, 1986; Petschek et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by the cuticle phenotype shown in Figure 12B.

claim: Following kni RNAi in M. abdita embryos, abdominal segments A1–7 merge.
source: Following kni RNAi in M. abdita embryos, abdominal segments A1–7 merge (Figure 12C).
evidence: This is supported by the cuticle phenotype shown in Figure 12C.

claim: The severe kni RNAi phenotype in M. abdita is very similar to the null mutant kni phenotype in D. melanogaster.
source: This severe kni RNAi phenotype is very similar to the null mutant kni phenotype in D. melanogaster (Nüsslein-Volhard and Wieschaus, 1980; Jürgens et al., 1984; Nauber et al., 1988).
evidence: This is based on comparison to published D. melanogaster mutant phenotypes.

claim: In severely affected M. abdita Kr knock-down cuticles, only the telson and A8, plus one or two additional abdominal segments are formed.
source: In severely affected M. abdita Kr knock-down cuticles, only the telson and A8, plus one or two additional abdominal segments are formed (putative A7, and sometimes A6; Figure 12D).
evidence: This is supported by the cuticle phenotype shown in Figure 12D.

claim: In kni knock-down embryos, a posterior expansion of the anterior hb domain is observed in 30 out of 54 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In kni knock-down embryos (Figure 6A–C) we observe a posterior expansion of the anterior hb domain (in 30 out of 54 RNAi-treated embryos) and an anterior expansion of posterior hb (35/52).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In kni knock-down embryos, an anterior expansion of posterior hb is observed in 35 out of 52 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In kni knock-down embryos (Figure 6A–C) we observe a posterior expansion of the anterior hb domain (in 30 out of 54 RNAi-treated embryos) and an anterior expansion of posterior hb (35/52).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The kni knock-down phenotype is stronger in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster kni mutants.
source: This phenotype is stronger than that of kni mutants in D. melanogaster, where only the anterior expansion of posterior hb has been observed but the anterior domain remains unaffected (Jäckle et al., 1986; Houchmandzadeh et al., 2002; Clyde et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on comparison to published D. melanogaster mutant phenotypes.

claim: In hb knock-down embryos, an anterior expansion of the abdominal kni domain is observed in 9 out of 14 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In hb knock-down embryos (Figure 6D–F), we observe an anterior expansion of the abdominal kni domain (9/14).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The anterior expansion of kni in M. abdita hb RNAi is considerably less pronounced than in D. melanogaster hb null mutants.
source: A similar expansion is seen in maternal and zygotic hb null mutants of D. melanogaster but is considerably more pronounced than in M. abdita (Hülskamp et al., 1990; Rothe et al., 1994; Clyde et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on comparison to published D. melanogaster mutant phenotypes.

claim: Kr is not down-regulated in M. abdita hb RNAi.
source: This could be due to the fact that Kr is not down-regulated in M. abdita hb RNAi (see below), while it is strongly reduced in D. melanogaster hb mutants (Hülskamp et al., 1990).
evidence: This is based on the RNAi expression data and comparison to D. melanogaster.

claim: In Kr knock-down embryos, expansion of the anterior gt domain is observed in 17 out of 20 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In Kr knock-down embryos (Figure 6G–I), we observe expansion of the anterior (17/20) and posterior (8/20) domains of gt into the central region of the embryo.
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In Kr knock-down embryos, expansion of the posterior gt domain is observed in 8 out of 20 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In Kr knock-down embryos (Figure 6G–I), we observe expansion of the anterior (17/20) and posterior (8/20) domains of gt into the central region of the embryo.
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Retraction defects of gt at the posterior pole region are detected in 11 out of 20 Kr knock-down embryos.
source: Surprisingly, we also detect retraction defects of gt at the posterior pole region in some embryos (11/20).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data.

claim: The retraction defect of gt in Kr knock-down embryos is unlikely to be direct, since Kr is not expressed in the posterior pole region at the relevant stages.
source: This effect is unlikely to be direct, since Kr is not expressed in this part of the embryo at the relevant stages of development (see Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern of Kr.

claim: Mutual repression between hb and kni is conserved between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: In summary, our results indicate that mutual repression between hb and kni is conserved, but the strength of these repressive interactions differs considerably between M. abdita and D. melanogaster
evidence: This is based on the RNAi knock-down results showing reciprocal effects.

claim: The strength of repressive interactions between hb and kni differs considerably between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: In summary, our results indicate that mutual repression between hb and kni is conserved, but the strength of these repressive interactions differs considerably between M. abdita and D. melanogaster: we detect weaker inhibition of kni by hb and stronger inhibition of hb by kni.
evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison of RNAi knock-down effects.

claim: There is weaker inhibition of kni by hb in M. abdita compared to D. melanogaster.
source: we detect weaker inhibition of kni by hb and stronger inhibition of hb by kni.
evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison of RNAi knock-down effects.

claim: There is stronger inhibition of hb by kni in M. abdita compared to D. melanogaster.
source: we detect weaker inhibition of kni by hb and stronger inhibition of hb by kni.
evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison of RNAi knock-down effects.

claim: The repressive asymmetry between hb and kni may contribute to the shift of the posterior boundary of anterior hb in M. abdita.
source: This repressive asymmetry is further supported by the alteration of hb expression following kni deregulation in gt RNAi embryos (see below), and may contribute to the shift of the posterior boundary of anterior hb, which is only observed in M. abdita but not in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed regulatory interactions and expression dynamics.

claim: The cross-repressive interactions between Kr and gt are very similar in M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: In addition, our results are consistent with the interpretation that the cross-repressive interactions between Kr and gt are very similar in both species
evidence: This is based on the RNAi knock-down results.

claim: In hb knock-down embryos, posterior gt fails to retract from the posterior pole in 24 out of 35 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In hb knock-down embryos (Figure 7A–C), posterior gt fails to retract from the posterior pole (24/35) or does not retract fully (4/35).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In gt knock-down embryos, the abdominal kni domain expands posteriorly in 11 out of 25 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In gt knock-down embryos (Figure 7D–F), the abdominal kni domain expands posteriorly (11/25).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In kni knock-down embryos, the central Kr domain shows a very pronounced expansion to the posterior in 26 out of 40 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In kni knock-down embryos (Figure 7G–I), the central Kr domain shows a very pronounced expansion to the posterior (26/40).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The effect of Kr on hb is stronger in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: Accordingly, the effect of Kr on hb is stronger in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNAi knock-down effects to published D. melanogaster mutant data.

claim: The anterior hb domain expands posteriorly in Kr knock-down embryos in 21 out of 41 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: The anterior hb domain expands posteriorly in Kr knock-down embryos (21/41) (Figure 7J–L).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In hb knock-down embryos, the central Kr domain expands towards the anterior in 24 out of 52 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In hb knock-down embryos, the central Kr domain expands towards the anterior (24/52; Figure 7Q,R).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 7.

claim: There is a strong asymmetry towards posterior-to-anterior neighbour repression in M. abdita.
source: In summary, our results indicate that there is a strong asymmetry towards posterior-to-anterior neighbour repression in M. abdita.
evidence: This is based on the RNAi knock-down results showing consistent posterior-to-anterior effects.

claim: Interactions involved in gap domain shifts are generally stronger in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: The less ambiguous nature of the evidence compared to D. melanogaster suggests that interactions involved in gap domain shifts are generally stronger in this species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clearer RNAi phenotypes observed in M. abdita.

claim: The difference in the repressive balance between Kr and hb is essential to explain the altered dynamics of boundary positioning between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: The observed difference in the repressive balance between Kr and hb, in particular, is essential to explain the altered dynamics of boundary positioning between the two species (see Conclusions).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the regulatory changes to the observed expression dynamics.

claim: Most terminal repression is carried out by tll, while the only known non-redundant role of hkb in gap gene patterning consists of positioning the posterior boundary of the posterior hb domain in D. melanogaster.
source: Most of this terminal repression is carried out by tll, while the only known non-redundant role of hkb in gap gene patterning consists of positioning the posterior boundary of the posterior hb domain (Ashyraliyev et al., 2009; Jaeger, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about terminal gap gene function in D. melanogaster.

claim: In M. abdita, tll and hkb play similar roles to D. melanogaster, although the amount of their respective regulatory contributions is altered.
source: In M. abdita, tll and hkb play similar roles, although the amount of their respective regulatory contributions is altered compared to D. melanogaster (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on the RNAi knock-down results shown in Figure 8.

claim: In tll knock-down embryos, the posterior hb domain is reduced in size in 12 out of 29 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In tll knock-down embryos, we find that the posterior hb domain is reduced in size (12/29) (Figure 8A2–3)
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 8.

claim: In hkb knock-down embryos, posterior hb is reduced in size in 21 out of 22 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In hkb knock-down embryos, we find that posterior hb is reduced in size (21/22) (Figure 8A4–5)
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 8.

claim: In tll hkb double knock-down embryos, posterior hb is strongly reduced in size in 15 out of 15 RNAi-treated embryos.
source: In tll hkb RNAi embryos, we find that posterior hb is strongly reduced in size (15/15) (Figure 8A6–7)
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi expression data shown in Figure 8.

claim: hkb may have a more prominent, and less redundant, role in regulating trunk gap genes in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that the regulatory effect of tll and hkb on trunk gap gene expression is similar in both species, although hkb may have a more prominent, and less redundant, role in regulating trunk gap genes in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster, as indicated by the synergistic effect on Kr and kni expression observed in tll hkb double knock-downs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the double knock-down results.

claim: The posterior boundary of the anterior hb domain shifts to the anterior over time in M. abdita, while it remains stationary throughout the blastoderm stage in D. melanogaster.
source: For instance, the posterior boundary of the anterior hb domain shifts to the anterior over time in M. abdita, while it remains stationary throughout the blastoderm stage in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data comparing the two species.

claim: The position and relative arrangement of gap domains converge in M. abdita and D. melanogaster towards the onset of gastrulation.
source: On the other hand, the output of the system is strongly conserved across 180 million years of evolution. The position and relative arrangement of gap domains converge in both species towards the onset of gastrulation.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Each gap domain is initially set up more posteriorly in M. abdita but 'catches up' with its equivalent in D. melanogaster through more pronounced anterior boundary shifts.
source: Each of these domains is initially set up more posteriorly, but 'catches up' with its equivalent in D. melanogaster through more pronounced anterior boundary shifts in M. abdita (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The timing of convergence of gap domain boundaries is delayed in the posterior of the embryo.
source: The timing of this convergence is delayed in the posterior of the embryo: posterior domain boundaries of posterior hb start to coincide at T8 (when this border becomes fully resolved in M. abdita), those of gt around T6, those of abdominal kni at T3, those of central Kr at T2, and those of anterior hb already around T1 (although the latter diverge again temporarily at later stages) (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Posterior gap domains appear further posterior in M. abdita due to the broadened distribution and influence of bcd.
source: Posterior gap domains appear further posterior—due to the broadened distribution and influence of bcd
evidence: This is an inference based on the bcd expression data and RNAi experiments.

claim: Posterior gap domains shift to the anterior later in M. abdita than in D. melanogaster due to the absence of maternal cad.
source: and shift to the anterior later than in D. melanogaster—due to the absence of maternal cad.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cad expression data and germ-line clone experiments.

claim: The delayed shifts are later compensated by pronounced, faster domain shifts in the second half of C14A in M. abdita.
source: This is later compensated by pronounced, faster domain shifts in the second half of C14A, an effect most clearly exhibited by Kr and gt (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The gap gene network in M. abdita reveals a stronger posterior-to-anterior bias in cross-repression between neighbouring domains compared to D. melanogaster.
source: Correspondingly, our knock-down analysis of the gap gene network in M. abdita reveals a stronger posterior-to-anterior bias in cross-repression between neighbouring domains (Figure 9; compare B to C).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi knock-down data and shown in Figure 9.

claim: Repression of hb by Kr and Kni is markedly stronger than the corresponding reverse interactions in M. abdita.
source: In this case, it is not only repression of hb by Kr, but also repression by Kni, which is markedly stronger than the corresponding reverse interactions (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi knock-down data and shown in Figure 9.

claim: The more pronounced domain shifts of hb and posterior boundaries in M. abdita are caused by increased posterior cross-regulatory bias.
source: Taken together, this suggests that the more pronounced domain shifts of hb and posterior boundaries in M. abdita are caused by increased posterior cross-regulatory bias.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the regulatory changes to the observed expression dynamics.

claim: Different developmental dynamics and regulatory interaction strengths in the gap gene network produce extremely similar patterns at the onset of gastrulation in M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Our analysis reveals how different developmental dynamics and regulatory interaction strengths in the gap gene network produce extremely similar patterns at the onset of gastrulation, despite significant differences in the initial phases of maternal co-ordinate and gap gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the expression and RNAi data.

claim: The observed phenomenon constitutes developmental system drift of a quantitative kind.
source: This constitutes developmental system drift of a quantitative kind: instead of changes in the qualitative nature of interactions (e.g., a switch from activation to repression), we observe neutral or compensatory evolution through tuning of regulatory interaction strengths.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of developmental system drift.

claim: A previous study proposed quantitative changes in signalling strength to account for the evolution of the vulval patterning system in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: While most published examples of developmental system drift are of the first, qualitative, kind, there is one previous study that proposed quantitative changes in signalling strength to account for the evolution of the vulval patterning system in Caenorhabditis elegans (Hoyos et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The precise molecular mechanism for quantitative changes in regulatory interactions remains unknown in M. abdita.
source: The precise molecular mechanism for such changes remains unknown in M. abdita at this point—and will be subject to future studies.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: Quantitative changes in regulatory interactions are likely based on altered numbers, affinities, or arrangements of transcription factor binding sites in cis-regulatory elements.
source: It is likely to be based on altered numbers, affinities, or arrangements of transcription factor binding sites in cis-regulatory elements (Levine, 2010; Wittkopp and Kalay, 2011) as observed in other dipteran lineages (Ludwig and Kreitman, 1995; Bonneton et al., 1997; Ludwig et al., 1998, 2000, 2005; Hancock et al., 1999; McGregor et al., 2001; Shaw et al., 2002; Gompel et al., 2005; Hare et al., 2008; Jeong et al., 2008; Williams et al., 2008; Peterson et al., 2009; Bradley et al., 2010; Frankel et al., 2011; Wunderlich et al., 2012; Paris et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation based on established knowledge and citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes at the sequence level that are not neutral at the level of cis-regulatory elements but lead to quantitative differences in interaction strength can lead to neutral drift at the systems- or network-level.
source: Here, we show that even these changes—that are not neutral at the level of cis-regulatory elements but lead to a quantitative difference in interaction strength—can lead to neutral drift if we consider their phenotypic effects at the systems- or network-level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: Quantitative system drift is a common feature of network evolution.
source: Based on the observed high turnover rates for the evolution of binding sites in various evolutionary lineages (McGregor et al., 2001; Dermitzakis and Clark, 2002; Ludwig, 2002; Costas et al., 2003; Dermitzakis et al., 2003; Moses et al., 2006; Yáñez-Cuna et al., 2013), we believe that such quantitative system drift is a common feature of network evolution.
evidence: This is speculation based on citations to previous studies on binding site evolution.

claim: Quantitative system drift supplies a mechanism for exploring alternative genotype spaces, increasing the range of mutationally accessible novel phenotypes.
source: It supplies a mechanism for exploring alternative genotype spaces, increasing the range of mutationally accessible novel phenotypes (Wagner, 2011; Jaeger and Monk, 2014)
evidence: This is speculation based on citations to theoretical work.

claim: Quantitative system drift allows for dynamically different alternative regulatory processes to evolve in specific developmental contexts.
source: and allows for dynamically different alternative regulatory processes to evolve in specific developmental contexts, such as that of segmentation (Oates et al., 2012; Richmond and Oates, 2012; Sarrazin et al., 2012; Jaeger and Sharpe, 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on citations to previous work on segmentation evolution.

claim: Quantitative system drift is likely to be important for neutral phenotypic evolution and for the de novo evolution of biological form.
source: Based on these considerations, quantitative system drift is likely to be important, not only for neutral phenotypic evolution but also for the de novo evolution of biological form.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and theoretical considerations.

claim: Quantitative system drift in early embryonic patterning networks provides an explanation for the developmental hourglass model.
source: Finally, quantitative system drift in early embryonic patterning networks, as reported here for the cyclorrhaphan gap gene system, provides an explanation for the developmental hourglass model (Seidel, 1960; Sander, 1983; Slack et al., 1993; Duboule, 1994; Raff, 1996).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the findings to the hourglass model, supported by citations.

claim: The developmental hourglass model predicts a minimum of morphological divergence during intermediate embryonic stages.
source: This model predicts a minimum of morphological divergence during intermediate embryonic stages.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the hourglass model.

claim: The developmental hourglass model has been confirmed at the level of gene expression in three recent studies.
source: It has been confirmed at the level of gene expression in three recent studies (Domazet-Lošo and Tautz, 2010; Kalinka et al., 2010; Quint et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Maternal co-ordinate and early gap gene expression differ significantly between M. abdita and D. melanogaster, but later converge to a common pattern.
source: We observe the same phenomenon in our explicitly spatio-temporal context: maternal co-ordinate and early gap gene expression differ significantly between species, but later converge to a common pattern (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative expression data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The knock-down analysis of the gap gene network in M. abdita provides causal regulatory explanations of how convergence is achieved at the gene network-level.
source: Our knock-down analysis of the gap gene network in M. abdita provides causal regulatory explanations of how this can be achieved at the gene network-level.
evidence: This is based on the RNAi knock-down experiments.

claim: M. abdita blastoderm stage embryos correspond to embryonic stages 4 and 5.
source: Blastoderm stage embryos of M. abdita—corresponding to embryonic stages 4 and 5 (Campos-Ortega and Hartenstein, 1997; Wotton et al., 2014)—were collected 4 hr (hrs) after egg laying.
evidence: This is supported by citations to staging schemes.

claim: All expression patterns are available online through the SuperFly database.
source: All the expression patterns presented here are available online through the SuperFly database (http://superfly.crg.eu) (Cicin-Sain et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes data availability.

claim: Two distinct dsRNA constructs were injected per gene for RNAi, one being the knock-down agent, the other serving as a control.
source: Two distinct dsRNA constructs were injected per gene, one being the knock-down agent, the other one—with conserved domains excluded—serving as a control.
evidence: This describes the RNAi methodology.
